articleTitle: Evaluation of large area die attach using acoustic microscopy
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on NDT Evaluation of Electronic Components and Assemblies
abstract: The technique chosen at Caswell for the analysis of die-bonds is acoustic microscopy. This is a reflection rather than transmission based technique, and has been used successfully for the nondestructive analysis of die-bonds up to 15 mm square. In this presentation, comparisons will be made between acoustic microscopy and other die-attach evaluation techniques. Examples will be shown of the way in which acoustic microscopy is used for bond evaluation and other assembly related activities.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Applications of high frequency ultrasonic inspection in microelectronics manufacturing
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on NDT Evaluation of Electronic Components and Assemblies
abstract: The problems involved in generating, detecting and quantifying ultrasound increase as the frequency increases, but the technology has kept pace and a range of sophisticated ultrasonic imaging equipment is now available. The techniques used can be broadly divided into two frequency ranges; namely 20-100 MHz and 100 MHz-1 GHz or more. The term 'scanning acousting microscopy' (SAM) is often used to describe imaging with high frequency ultrasound but purists may argue that this term should be applied only to a specific method of imaging, usually using frequencies of over 100 MHz. As the frequency increases the penetration falls and the resolution increases. In the 20-100 MHz range features of around 20-30 mu m can be resolved, with penetration of up to 10 mms or so in some materials. At the top of the 100 MHz-1 GHz range the resolution can be sub-micrometre, but a penetration of only a few micrometres is possible. The applications described here are all in the 20-75 MHz range, where a variety of techniques and measurement methods can be employed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Airborne ultrasonic inspection at 2 MHz; its application to SMT
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on NDT Evaluation of Electronic Components and Assemblies
abstract: Airborne ultrasonics offers certain advantages in inspection systems. Compared with vision systems, the signal acquisition time can be much shorter, signal processing is much simpler, and range information is obtained directly, rather than by complex triangulation methods. This ability to measure distance to an object, or the difference between two distances, makes ultrasonic techniques the obvious choice for many inspection situations. The advantage of airborne ultrasonics over conventional NDT ultrasonics is, of course, that no water bath or other liquid couplant is required. In the work described here, continuous-transmission frequency modulation (CTFM) is used with 2 MHz transducers to achieve a distance-measuring resolution in air of less than 25 mu m (0.001 inch).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Quest for an NDT method to detect marginal ESD damage to ICs
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on NDT Evaluation of Electronic Components and Assemblies
abstract: The magnitude of the static charge built up in a typical working environment ranges from 100 volts to 20 kV. It this is discharged through an integrated circuit it may result in gate oxide breakdown in MOS devices and short or open circuits in metal tracks leading to device failure. Failure in TTL is due to breakdown of the reverse biased junction as a result of impact ionisation and subsequent Joule heating. To reduce the likelihood of static damage, special handling procedures are followed as prescribed by BS 5783. However the level of protection achieved is at best a function of how rigorously the guidelines are obeyed. A non-destructive test is described to evaluate an integrated circuits' (IC) exposure to static damage events.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Backdriving-an update on the latest research
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on NDT Evaluation of Electronic Components and Assemblies
abstract: This paper describes the first and second phases of the research programme undertaken by the UK MOD (PE), with funding assistance from industry, to define the 'safe' limits for backdriving or node-forcing. The output from this work is to be released as an Interim UK Defence Standard, to guide Contractors and ATE Vendors, planned for mid-1990.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
